newsitem.title: USA: US 30-yr mortgage rates fall sixth consecutive wk.
newsitem.headline: US 30-yr mortgage rates fall sixth consecutive wk.

text.p: The average interest rate on U.S. 30-year fixed-rate mortgages fell to 7.52 percent in the week ending November 29, a sixth consecutive weekly decline, the Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corp said Wednesday.
Freddie Mac said the 30-year has not been lower since the week ended March 8, 1996, when the average was 7.38 percent. Last week's 30-year rate was 7.53 percent.
Fifteen-year loans also fell a sixth consecutive week to an average 7.04 percent, the lowest since a rate of 6.87 percent in the March 8 week. Last week's 15-year rate averaged 7.06 percent.
Adjustable rate mortgages inched upward to an average 5.50 percent from 5.48 percent last week.
A year ago, the 30-year rate averaged 7.33 percent, the 15-year 6.85 percent, and the ARM 5.60 percent.

"With 30-year fixed-rate mortgages settling around 7.5 percent, we anticipate that the ARM percentage of home purchases will begin to decline from its year-round high of 33 percent," Frank Nothaft, Freddie Mac deputy chief economist, said.
"We have generally found that families prefer the certainty of a fixed-rate mortgage when interest rates are as low as they are today," Nothaft added.
On Monday the National Assocation of Realtors said U.S. October sales of existing homes fell 1.5 percent to a 3.97 million unit annual rate.

Freddie Mac said lenders charged an average 1.8 percent in fees and points on 30-year loans and 1.7 percent on 15-year loans, both unchanged from last week. They charged 1.4 percent on the ARM, also unchanged from last week.
